## Discussion

The main lesson of this study is methodological as much as empirical. The comparison between the iEEG atlas and source-reconstructed HD-EEG does not reduce to a single question of whether one dataset reproduces the other. Rather, it shows that different spectral techniques turn the same data into different comparison objects. A band-power map, a fitted peak, a residual after aperiodic correction, a dominant centre frequency, and an aperiodic exponent are all summaries of the spectrum, and they are not interchangeable.

This matters because the two modalities did not differ only in overall quality or strength of signal. Source-reconstructed HD-EEG produced a narrow, high-amplitude alpha-dominated pattern, whereas the iEEG atlas showed a broader distribution of peaks across alpha, beta, low gamma, and high gamma, together with a different aperiodic shape. Depending on the descriptor, this contrast can look like partial cross-modal recovery, failure to recover high-frequency rhythms, or a change in the apparent oscillatory pattern after aperiodic correction. The result is therefore not one stable answer hidden behind several analyses, but a demonstration that the answer depends on how "oscillation," "frequency", and "agreement" are operationalised.

The alpha pattern is the most robust point of convergence across descriptors, but the interpretation of beta and gamma activity changes across relative power, fitted peaks, and subtraction residuals. The aperiodic exponent is not a fixed property waiting to be read from the spectrum either: in iEEG it depends strongly on whether the spectrum is treated as fixed or knee-shaped, while in source HD-EEG it is more stable across methods. The chapter therefore uses the cross-modal comparison not only to ask what HD-EEG can recover from iEEG, but also to show which spectral conclusions are robust to the analytical route used to obtain them.

### Branching Paths

This chapter set out as a narrower comparison and widened as the surrounding methodological literature did. Several of the studies that now anchor the analysis were published after the project began, and the scope had to be closed at some point rather than tracked indefinitely. The analysis has the structure of a garden of forking paths [@gelman2013GardenForkingPaths]: many defensible operational choices were available before the results were interpreted, in how oscillations are extracted, how frequency is represented, and how cross-modal agreement is summarised. Rather than commit to one pipeline, we report several branches and ask which conclusions survive across them.

Two choices shaped the analysis enough to be worth stating directly. First, we avoided relative band power as a basis for inference. Relative powers are compositional: within each channel the bands are normalised to a fixed total, so they cannot vary independently and ordinary correlation across them is not valid [@filzmoser2012CorrelationAnalysisCompositional]. We retained the untransformed maps only as a descriptive summary and carried inference with the aperiodic-separated peak descriptors instead. Second, summarising a multivariate, multi-region, multi-band comparison is itself a data-reduction problem, and much of the work is carried by visualisation: several figures present closely related information from different angles because no single reduction captures the comparison without discarding something that matters elsewhere.

### What is recovered, what is not

The strongest cross-modal signal is alpha, and the preservation of regional structure is band-dependent. On uncorrected relative-power maps, regional agreement was clearest in alpha (r = 0.60) and weaker in delta (r = 0.42), with essentially no correspondence in theta (r = 0.13), only weak agreement in beta (r = 0.30), and an anti-correlation in gamma (r = −0.29). The same pattern held once oscillations were modelled explicitly and the aperiodic background removed: cross-modal agreement of regional peak prevalence was confined to the low and mid bands (alpha ρ = 0.60, beta ρ = 0.47) against delta ρ = 0.04, theta ρ = −0.07 and gamma ρ = −0.25. That the uncorrected and aperiodic-corrected descriptors agree on where preservation holds is the clearest single result of the chapter: large-scale spatial organisation is partly recoverable in source HD-EEG, but the recovery is concentrated in alpha and the low-frequency range and breaks down at high frequencies. The negative gamma correspondence is consistent with the high-frequency HD-EEG signal being dominated by a shallow aperiodic tail and noise floor rather than by physiological gamma.

The descriptor used to detect peaks was itself unstable, which is part of the finding rather than an aside. The k-means clustering solution, the no-peak reference set, and the data-driven interval definition all shifted with reasonable changes to preprocessing and fitting range, and the 4% power rule of the original atlas did not transfer to the source-reconstructed spectra: applied to HD-EEG it over-segmented the high-frequency tail, a consequence of the unit-power normalisation rather than of physiological structure. Because the clustering descriptor was not robust to these choices, we did not carry it forward to the aperiodic-corrected spectra and characterised oscillatory content with the more stable per-band parametrised-peak descriptor, which needs neither a clustering step nor a no-peak reference. The instability is therefore not noise around a true answer; it is a reason to prefer one operationalisation over another.

The posterior-to-anterior frequency gradient recovered here is consistent with reports from MEG using both parameterised [@mahjoory2020FrequencyGradientHuman] and non-parametric data-driven [@arana2026MEGLowdensityEEG] approaches, and from iEEG using spectral parameterisation [@kalamangalam2020NeurophysiologicalBrainMap]. Its partial preservation in HD-EEG extends the pattern across an additional modality and a coarser spatial resolution regime. The cross-modal recovery of alpha specifically is consistent with alpha being tied to laminar and feedback/feedforward circuit architecture [@jensen2026AlphaRhythmPhysiology], implying that at least some of the regional oscillatory structure recovered here reflects broader circuit organisation rather than isolated narrowband generators. This places the result alongside two adjacent literatures while marking what is new: Janiukstyte et al. [-@janiukstyte2023NormativeBrainMapping] reported comparable spatial gradients in scalp EEG but without joint aperiodic treatment, and Afnan et al. [-@afnan2023ValidatingMEGSource] reported partial recovery in MEG with lateral regions recovered more accurately than deep or medial ones. The present chapter adds a non-invasive modality more vulnerable to source mixing than MEG, and treats periodic and aperiodic features together.

### Aperiodic correction changes oscillatory interpretation

Separating periodic from aperiodic activity does not simply raise or lower cross-modal agreement; it changes which apparent differences are real. The two modalities required different aperiodic models. In the iEEG atlas the knee model was decisively preferred (median R² rising from 0.93 to 0.98, per-channel MSE falling by 77%, median ΔBIC ≈ −225 with 96% of channels strongly favouring the knee), whereas in source HD-EEG the knee improved fit only marginally (R² 0.942 to 0.948, MSE down ~7%) and the formal ΔBIC preference was fragile under subject-level resampling. We therefore fit the knee for iEEG and the fixed model for HD-EEG, so the two residuals are produced by different models — a fact that matters for how their difference is read.

Read through the measure that does not depend on the accuracy of the aperiodic fit — the modelled peak amplitude — the modalities differ in a contiguous beta/low-gamma band (~25-48 Hz, iEEG higher) across most lobes, agree in a parietal alpha cluster (~10-12 Hz, HD higher), and differ again in occipital high gamma (iEEG higher). The detrended residual reproduces the beta excess but adds a broad high-frequency cluster (~55-80 Hz) in which HD-EEG appears systematically higher across every lobe. That cluster is present in the residual and absent from the modelled measure, which identifies it as aperiodic-tail or noise leakage rather than a rhythm — exactly the conflation that detrending is expected to produce when the aperiodic fit is misestimated [@castanheira2025QuantifyingRhythmicArrhythmic]. We therefore read the modelled-peak comparison as the substantive cross-modal result, and the high-frequency residual difference as an artefact of the background rather than a difference in oscillatory activity.

This has a direct bearing on prior cross-modal work. The high-frequency disagreement that survives in band power and detrended spectra can be an aperiodic artefact, so normative maps built on band power without aperiodic correction [@janiukstyte2023NormativeBrainMapping] may report cross-modal differences at high frequency that do not reflect rhythms. Afnan et al. [-@afnan2023ValidatingMEGSource] found that MEG-iEEG agreement improved after aperiodic components were removed; the present result is consistent with that direction but more specific about the mechanism: correction did not improve overlap uniformly across bands, it removed a spurious high-frequency component and left the alpha correspondence standing.

### Methodological dependencies of aperiodic estimates

The aperiodic exponent reported for iEEG is a modelling choice as much as a property of the spectrum. The knee and fixed models returned very different iEEG exponents (median χ = 3.30 vs 1.94) that correlated only moderately across channels (r = 0.49), because forcing a single line through a spectrum with a genuine knee biases the exponent low by a channel-specific amount. In source HD-EEG, where the knee is essentially absent, the two exponents nearly coincided (0.94 vs 0.93; r = 0.88). The fitting range mattered in the same asymmetric way: narrowing the fixed-mode range from 1-80 Hz to 1-45 Hz lowered the iEEG exponent by a near-constant offset (mean Δχ ≈ +0.47, broadly distributed across regions), while leaving the HD-EEG exponent essentially unchanged (Δχ ≈ −0.04). Cross-modal exponent comparisons must therefore hold the fitting range fixed, and are only interpretable below ~45 Hz, where the two modalities behave comparably.

Two checks bound how far these dependencies are artefacts of the parameterisation. In HD-EEG the specparam fixed-mode exponent and the IRASA fractal exponent agreed almost perfectly over the same band (r = 0.97), so the recovered slope is method-independent in the source data: the cross-modal and range effects are properties of the spectra, not of specparam. The remaining dependency is the functional form itself, since the same data fit with a 1/f versus a knee (Lorentzian-shaped) aperiodic model yield different exponents whenever a knee is present. These results sit alongside reports that the exponent depends on the estimation range [@boncompte2026AperiodicExponentBrain; @gerster2022SeparatingNeuralOscillations; @wilson2024ModelSelectionSpectral], and alongside Ameen et al. [-@ameen2025TemporallyResolvedAnalyses], who, working on this same iEEG-plus-HD-EEG dataset in sleep, found that whether the knee is included substantially affects stage-dependent variation. Our wakefulness result — iEEG needs the knee, HD-EEG does not — is consistent with theirs and reinforces the case for selecting the aperiodic mode per modality rather than imposing one form across both.

### Methodological caveats and limitations

The limitations of this chapter fall into three groups: data-level constraints on the comparison itself, methodological dependencies of the parameterisation, and limits on what can be inferred from convergence across metrics.

**Data-level.** No simultaneously recorded iEEG-and-scalp dataset was available, so the comparison is between two different cohorts recorded under different conditions, and modality cannot be cleanly separated from condition or population. The Frauscher iEEG atlas was recorded with eyes closed, whereas the HD-EEG dataset was recorded with eyes open. Eye state affects oscillatory activity, most strongly posterior alpha power, and may also affect the aperiodic exponent and offset (Geller et al. 2014). Where cross-modal agreement is observed, it is therefore observed despite differences in recording condition; where it is weak, modality and condition cannot be fully separated with these data. The aggregation structures also differ: 1772 channels across 106 patients in iEEG versus 1444 virtual sensors across 19 subjects in HD-EEG, so per-region statistics are pooled differently in the two modalities, and this asymmetry should be kept in mind when interpreting between-region differences. Finally, the atlas was recorded in patients with refractory epilepsy; although only channels in non-epileptogenic regions were retained, the extent to which these spectral features generalise to non-epileptic populations is a known limitation of the reference [@frauscher2018AtlasNormalIntracranial].

**Method-level.** Spectral parameterisation depends on the assumed aperiodic functional form, the fitting frequency range, and the peak-detection thresholds; the chapter addresses this dependency directly through the stability analyses above, but the estimates should still be read as conditional on those choices [@donoghue2021MethodologicalConsiderationsStudying]. A subset of source-reconstructed spectra additionally showed near-flat slopes with exponents close to zero and low fit quality (R² < 0.70), no clear 1/f structure, and where peaks were present they were confined to the beta range. These are unlikely to reflect genuine neural dynamics with an unusually flat broadband component; more plausibly they arise from source labels that receive little coherent signal after inverse modelling, so the reconstructed time course is dominated by spatially smoothed noise or leakage from neighbouring regions [@tait2021SystematicEvaluationSource]. Biophysical modelling suggests that high-frequency broadband power in scalp EEG may not be neural in origin [@brake2025ContributionsActionPotentials; @brake2024NeurophysiologicalBasisAperiodic], and this concern carries over to source-reconstructed data, where the inverse solution cannot recover signal absent at the sensor level. Fitting the fixed aperiodic model to such spectra yields nominally valid parameters that should not be read as cortical broadband dynamics [@wilson2024ModelSelectionSpectral; @gerster2022SeparatingNeuralOscillations]. Sources with R² below 0.90 were flagged and the sensitivity of regional results to their inclusion or exclusion was assessed. <!-- TODO: state the outcome of this sensitivity check — the Results report the flagging (99.7% iEEG vs 74.0% HD passed R²>0.9) but I could not find the actual inclusion/exclusion result stated, so I did not write one in. --> A further confound at this level is waveform shape: non-sinusoidal rhythms generate harmonics that specparam can fit as separate peaks, which can inflate apparent high-band peak counts in either modality.

**Inferential.** The chapter reports convergence across multiple comparison methods — the Afnan overlap, Spearman correlation across regions, peak-prevalence differences, and the hierarchical Bayesian regression — rather than committing to a single pipeline. Each metric encodes a different assumption about what counts as agreement: whether one modality is treated as ground truth, whether comparison is made at the level of medians or full distributions, and whether scale or rank is preserved. Convergence across these metrics is reassuring but does not establish that they are interchangeable under conditions where modalities diverge more sharply than they do here. A controlled simulation in which the underlying spatial pattern is known would help characterise when the metrics agree and where they diverge, and is left for future work.

### Conclusion

This chapter does not claim a definitive validation of source-reconstructed HD-EEG against intracranial EEG. It asks a narrower and more answerable pair of questions: whether large-scale regional spectral organisation is preserved well enough to support cautious cross-modal comparison, and whether separating oscillatory from broadband components changes that comparison. On those terms the chapter should be judged not by whether it removes all ambiguity, but by whether it makes the sources of ambiguity explicit and tests their consequences.

What it shows is threefold. Regional spectral organisation is partly preserved across the two modalities, with the preservation concentrated in alpha and the low-frequency range and breaking down at high frequencies. Accounting for the aperiodic background changes the interpretation of oscillatory findings rather than uniformly improving agreement, and in particular reveals that an apparent high-frequency cross-modal difference is an artefact of the background rather than a rhythm. And the aperiodic exponent — at least in iEEG — depends materially on the model form and fitting range used to estimate it. Taken together, these results underscore the need for cautious, model-aware interpretation of parameterised spectral measures in human EEG, and the value of examining oscillatory and aperiodic features jointly rather than reading either in isolation.

The contribution to the wider validation effort is specific in three ways. It uses HD-EEG rather than MEG, which is far more widely available but more vulnerable to volume conduction and source mixing; the validation of source-reconstructed scalp electrophysiology against direct intracranial measurement has so far been carried out mostly with MEG [@afnan2023ValidatingMEGSource]. It examines oscillatory and aperiodic features jointly rather than band power alone, as in earlier normative scalp-EEG maps [@janiukstyte2023NormativeBrainMapping]. And it reports convergence across several comparison methods rather than one pipeline, which strengthens the conclusions where convergence holds and flags where it does not.

What the chapter does not claim is equally specific, and this is where its practical reach ends. It does not claim that normative HD-EEG maps are ready for clinical biomarker use, nor that the patterns reported here generalise across populations, ages, or recording conditions, nor that a source-reconstructed HD-EEG map can replace iEEG for fine-grained regional analysis; each of these needs dedicated work. What it offers is a characterisation of which features of regional spectral organisation are recoverable from source-reconstructed HD-EEG, and which are sensitive to the assumptions of the pipeline used to obtain them. The practical payoff — knowing which non-invasive spectral measures can be trusted regionally, and under which modelling choices — is a step that others, designing biomarker or mapping studies, would still need to take up and test in their own data.

### Further steps

Beyond the controlled-simulation evaluation of cross-modal metrics noted above, two extensions follow directly from the present design. A simultaneously recorded iEEG-and-scalp dataset would let modality, recording condition, and population be separated, which the present two-cohort comparison cannot do. And the same joint periodic/aperiodic comparison could be run between reconstructed sources and other modalities at the sensor level, and across differing parcellation atlases, to test how far the recoverable structure reported here depends on the specific atlas and source model used.
